Broadland's population increased by around 7,100 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 130,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Broadland increased by 5.7%, from just over 124,600 in 2011 to around 131,700 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of the East of England (8.3%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Broadland was home to around 1.7 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 1.6 in 2011. This area was among the lowest 30% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Broadland than across the East of England

An older Broadland

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Broadland increased by three years, from 45 to 48 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the East of England as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by just over 2,900 (an increase of 20.3%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 3,200 (12.0% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 1.6 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Broadland stood out from other areas for housing

The percentage of households in the social rented sector increased in Broadland, but fell across England.

In Broadland, the percentage of households in the social rented sector rose from 8.6% in 2011 to 9.7% in 2021, while across England it fell from 17.7% to 17.1%. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 15.7% to 15.5%.

Private renting in Broadland increased from 10.3% to 12.3%, while the rate of home ownership decreased from 79.4% to 77.1%.

The rate of social renting in Broadland increased by 1.2 percentage points

Religion in Broadland

In 2021, 44.5% of Broadland residents reported having "No religion", up from 28.0% in 2011. The rise of 16.5 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Broadland. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the East of England, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.9% to 40.2%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 47.7% of people in Broadland described themselves as Christian (down from 63.3%), while 6.2% did not state their religion (down from 7.4% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 44.5% of usual residents in Broadland reported having "No religion"

Unpaid care in Broadland

In 2021, 5.0% of Broadland residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.9% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, 1.5% of residents (aged five years and over) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.2% in 2011. The proportion of Broadland residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care remained at 2.3%.

This area had the region’s joint third highest proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (alongside Maldon). Across the region, only South Cambridgeshire (5.1%) and Three Rivers (5.1%) had a higher proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Broadland decreased by 2.9 percentage points

Broadland residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 121,600 Broadland residents said they were born in England. This represented 92.3% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 116,600 in 2011, which at the time represented 93.6% of Broadland's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just over 1,500 Broadland residents reporting this country of birth (1.2%). This figure was down from around 1,600 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.3% of the population of Broadland.

The number of Broadland residents born in Wales remained close to 850 between the last two census (from 0.7% of the local population in 2011 to 0.6% in 2021)

In 2021, 92.3% of Broadland residents reported their country of birth as England

Health in Broadland

In 2021, 48.2% of Broadland residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 46.4% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 36.6% to 35.6%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Broadland residents describing their health as "very bad" was 0.8% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" was 3.2% (similar to 2011).

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very bad health in Broadland decreased by 0.2 percentage points

National identity in Broadland

In 2021, 2.8% of Broadland residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 1.9% in 2011.

In 2021, 0.9% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.4% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Broadland that identified as "British only" increased from 13.9% to 56.7%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the East of England (2.1 percentage points, from 6.9% to 9.0%) than in Broadland (0.9 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Broadland increased by 0.9 percentage points

Fewer couples without children

Of Broadland households, 20.0% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 22.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in five households (18.6%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 20.1% in 2011. The percentage of single family households including a couple living with only non-dependent children decreased from 6.8% to 6.6%.

The decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children was greater in Broadland (2.2 percentage points) than across the East of England (1.8 percentage points, from 19.0% to 17.2%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.9 percentage points, from 17.6% to 16.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Broadland decreased by 2.2 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Broadland residents aged 16 years and over, 28.6% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 24.5% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in two people (51.7%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 55.8% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Broadland that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.5% to 10.3%.

This area had the region’s joint second lowest percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership (alongside Babergh). Across the region, only North Norfolk, with 27.2%, had a lower percentage.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Broadland increased by 4.1 percentage points

Change in employment

Of Broadland residents aged 16 years and over, 55.5% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 57.9% in 2011.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in Broadland (2.4 percentage points) than across the East of England (1.1 percentage points, from 58.4% to 57.3%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Broadland decreased by 2.4 percentage points

Working hours in Broadland

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week changed very little in Broadland, while the percentage increased in nearby North Norfolk.

In Broadland, the percentage of adults in employment working 15 hours or less stayed close to 11.4% between the last two censuses. During the same period, the percentage in nearby North Norfolk increased from 12.1% to 14.4%.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Broadland fell from 13.0% to 10.8%, while the percentage of adults in employment who worked 31 to 48 hours increased from 54.5% to 55.9%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

In 2021, 11.4% of usual residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week in Broadland

Disability in Broadland

In 2021, 6.4% of Broadland residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 7.3% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under one in nine people (10.6%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 9.7% in 2011. The proportion of Broadland residents who were not disabled remained at 83.0%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Broadland (0.9 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East of England (1.2 percentage points, from 7.8% to 6.6%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Broadland decreased by 0.9 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Broadland

In 2021, 1.4% of Broadland residents identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category, up from 0.9% in 2011. The 0.5 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the East of England, the percentage of people from "Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups" increased from 1.9% to 2.8%, while across England the percentage increased from 2.3% to 3.0%.

In 2021, 96.3% of people in Broadland identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 97.7% in 2011), while 1.4% identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category (compared with 1.0% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category increased from 0.3% in 2011 to 0.5% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
